content.title: About
content.content: Cheese flavored corn snacks (Cheetos) are crunchy bites made from cornmeal dough that are coated with a savory cheese seasoning. They have a distinctive cheesy taste, light airy texture, and a bright orange hue. The snack is popular as a quick bite and is often found in cinemas, parties, and school cafeterias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Cheetos product was launched by Frito‑Lay in 1948.
The cheese flavor is created using a blend of natural and artificial flavorings, including cheese powder and spices.
Several flavor variants exist: original cheese, Flamin’ Hot, cheddar baked, and lime.
In the 2020s, the brand introduced the extremely spicy Flamin’ Hot Cheetos, the hottest in the line‑up.
Cheetos are often used in culinary experiments: crushed as a coating, mixed into dough for cookies, or used as a garnish for dishes.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The snack provides carbohydrates that are rapidly digested, delivering an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Contains vitamin A precursors
items.content: The orange color comes from beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A important for vision.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Cornmeal contributes a modest amount of iron, which supports blood formation.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: Strong cheese flavor can increase feelings of fullness and help curb overeating.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: Cheetos often contain a notable amount of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Fried corn snacks are rich in fats and calories, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Allergy to corn or dairy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn starch or cheese‑based flavorings.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: The product frequently includes artificial colors and flavorings that can cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the snack straight from the bag as a quick bite. It can be sprinkled over salads for crunch, used as a topping for casseroles, or crushed and incorporated into cookie or muffin batter to add a cheesy flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bag in a cool, dry place and reseal tightly after opening to prevent moisture absorption. For longer storage, transfer to an airtight container. Exposure to heat or humidity will make the snacks lose their crispness and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double Hamburger is a signature fast‑food item consisting of two medium beef patties (171 g each), a bun, lettuce, a slice of cheese, pickles, onions and the chain’s special sauce. It is designed for those who crave a hearty, flavorful meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Each patty weighs about 171 g, making the portion substantially larger than a standard burger.
The Double Hamburger is often sold as part of a combo with fries and a drink.
The recipe uses premium beef and a blend of spices that highlight the natural meat flavor.
The bun is lightly toasted to keep a crisp crust while remaining soft inside.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Two patties provide roughly 40 g of protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The burger supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates offers a quick source of energy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A Double Hamburger can exceed 800 kcal, so it should be accounted for in daily intake.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: A notable amount of saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt in the sauce and pickles can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains dairy (cheese) and gluten (bun), which are common allergens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Double Hamburger is typically eaten by hand, holding the bottom bun. It can be complemented with fries, extra sauce, or fresh vegetables according to personal preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared Double Hamburger should be kept refrigerated and consumed within 2 hours. For longer storage, reheat in an oven or microwave to restore the bun’s crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Fish is an aquatic vertebrate that provides a valuable source of high‑quality protein, omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals. Steaming (1027) preserves most of its nutrients, resulting in a tender, juicy, and easily digestible product.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Steaming retains up to 90 % of vitamin D, which is important for bone health.
Steamed fish keeps its natural flavor and aroma without added fats.
There are more than 30,000 marine and freshwater fish species, but only a small fraction are widely used in cuisine.
Omega‑3 fatty acids in fish help lower blood triglyceride levels.
Steamed fish is a staple in many Asian dishes such as dim sum and sushi.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support heart, brain, and eye health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish contains B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Selenium, iodine, and phosphorus in fish aid thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Steaming requires no added oil, keeping saturated fat content minimal.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species can accumulate mercury and cadmium; choosing smaller species and moderating intake is advisable.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth.

items.title: High sodium in some preparations
items.content: Salted or cured fish can increase sodium intake, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed fish can be served as a main dish, added to salads, soups, rice or noodle bowls. It pairs well with lemon, fresh herbs (dill, parsley), and light sauces based on yogurt or soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh fish refrigerated at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container and use within 2 days. Frozen fish should be stored at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for a strong ammonia‑like odor; discard if present.

pizza-with-extra-meat-medium-crust.title: Pizza with extra meat, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with extra meat and a medium crust is a classic Italian pizza topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and a generous mix of meats such as ham, sausage, bacon, and beef. The medium‑thick dough provides a balance between a crisp edge and a soft interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The modern pizza originated in Naples in the 18th century.
Meat toppings are often called a “meat mix” and can include up to five different types of meat.
Medium crust is typically baked at 220‑250 °C, yielding a golden‑brown crust.
The combination of tomato sauce and meat enhances iron absorption from the meat.
In the United States, meat‑topped pizza ranks among the top‑10 fast‑food favorites.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and tomato sauce provide vitamins B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Lycopene in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain diseases.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The abundance of meat and cheese makes this pizza calorie‑dense; moderation is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meats and cheese contain saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sausage and ham are often high in salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose alternative cheeses.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into portions. Fresh basil, oregano, or a light drizzle of hot sauce can enhance flavor. To reduce calories, remove some meat or substitute part of the cheese with a lower‑fat option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.
